title: Precision Mixer: runtime adapter for head- and token-aware INT8/FP8 routing
creator: Ava Patel
description:
Background: We routinely choose a single precision path (INT8 or FP8) for a given model runtime. That simplifies kernel scheduling but forces a global trade-off between latency/cost and quality. On production workloads with mixed prompt distributions, selective precision (per-head or per-token) can offer better economics while keeping regressions under control.

Goal: Implement a runtime "Precision Mixer" adapter that: (1) selects kernel precision (INT8 vs FP8 vs FP16) at a per-layer/per-head or short token-span granularity, (2) minimizes dequantization overhead by delaying or batching dequant ops and using in-kernel cast paths when available, and (3) exposes telemetry to tie quality regressions to precision choices so we can safely roll out.

Success criteria (initial):
- p50 token latency no worse than current INT8 baseline on typical chat workloads (+/- 5%).
- p99 latency increase <= 10% for the canary traffic.
- Token compute cost reduction of >= 12% vs FP16 baseline on the targeted workload mix.
- No measurable quality regression on our regression test set (delta-quality < 1% for top metrics).

Scope & approach:
1) Offline profiler: build a short profiler that runs representative traces and emits a per-layer/tokendistribution cost-quality frontier (latency vs quality metric). Output is a small JSON artifact that drives heuristics.
2) Heuristic adapter: implement a compact runtime policy that maps (model, layer, head, token-context window) -> precision decision. Start with a rule-based scoring function: importance_score = (head_entropy * recent_logits_magnitude) and map thresholds to precision levels.
3) Kernel selector changes: extend the kernel arbitration to accept a precision plan for the active token batch. Support: fused INT8-attn kernels, FP8 microkernels, and a path that avoids eager dequant by keeping KV entries in quantized form and only dequantizing when the downstream kernel requires it.
4) KV cache representation: add a lightweight shadow descriptor that tracks whether a cached entry is in quantized or dequantized form to prevent repeated dequant ops for streaming sessions.
5) Telemetry & safety: add rollup metrics (precision mix by model and route, latency deltas, token-cost estimates) and integrate with Optimize's regression gates.

Implementation milestones: 1) Spike & profiler (week 1-2), 2) kernel selector prototype + unit tests (week 2-4), 3) KV-shadow + streaming correctness tests (week 3-5), 4) bench + quality eval + internal canary (week 5-6), 5) wide canary + rollback automation (week 7-9).

Risks & trade-offs:
- Complexity: head/token-level routing increases scheduler state and may harm throughput if decisions fragment batches. We'll mitigate with batching-friendly heuristics (coalesce adjacent tokens with same plan, fall back to model-level choice under high concurrency).
- Dequant overhead: naive dequant can erase benefits. We will instrument and prefer "lazy dequant" where the system records quantized tensors and only materializes floats for kernels that cannot accept quantized input.
- Quality regressions: per-token precision may produce subtle distributional shifts. We'll gate any traffic changes with automated evals against pinned prompt sets and per-route quality thresholds.

Open questions:
- Best continuous scoring function for head importance; initial experiments will compare entropy-based vs gradient-approx importance proxies.
- How to expose debug visualization in Console for per-request precision traces without overwhelming retention budgets.

Artifacts & links: 
- Design doc: https://redwood.atlassian.net/wiki/spaces/RUN/pages/Precision+Mixer+Design (internal Confluence)
- Profiler proto: drive: https://drive.redwood.ai/drive/folders/precision-mixer/profiler (private)
- Benchmark board (internal): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/bench/quant-mixer
- Spike PR (draft): https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/7321

Rollout plan: Start with "lab" models on a dedicated cluster. If bench results align with success criteria, deploy a 1% canary for a low-volume customer route and watch: latency p50/p99, quality regression alarms (Optimize), token-cost delta, and error rates. If stable, increase to 5% then 20% with automatic rollback if regressions detected.

Notes: This ticket focuses on runtime/kernel-level changes and lightweight policy heuristics. Follow-up tickets will explore ML-learned routing policies and model-aware calibration curves for precision vs quality.

2026-03-05 - Diego Mendez: Implemented kernel selector hooks for per-layer precision plan. Added unit tests for fallbacks. Observed 6% p50 latency regression on microbench when enabling per-token decisions; batching coalescing reduced that to 1.5%.

2026-03-07 - Keiko Sato (Senior Eng review): Reviewed approach. Concern: shadow KV adds memory churn. Suggest using compressed descriptor and amortize conversions across session buckets. Also requested an explicit test for seq-len=2048 streaming workloads.
2026-03-08 - PM note (Liam O'Connor): Please keep canary plan conservative; prioritize customer routes flagged as cost-sensitive. Add a label to allow opt-out by sales on dedicated customers.

2026-03-09 - Diego Mendez: Created draft PR for runtime changes (https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/7321). CI flaky on new scheduler tests; investigating interleaving with existing microbatching code. Tagged ENG-21458 as dependency for cache telemetry hooks.

2026-03-10 - QA: Synthetic regressions check passed on our predefined eval set. Noted a 0.9% delta on perplexity for a few prompts—within threshold but will add additional A/B target cases before canary.
Next steps: finish CI stability, add streaming seq-len stress tests, and prepare canary dashboard (Grafana panel link above).
